meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that's the stuff life is made of'?
meta.ogDescription: A Franklin attribution that actually checks out — from Poor Richard's Almanack (1746), repeated verbatim in "The Way to Wealth" (1758).

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1706–1790 · American founding father, printer & author of Poor Richard’s Almanack
answer.sourceLine: This is a rare case where a Franklin attribution holds up: the maxim first appeared in his Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1746 and he restated it verbatim in his celebrated 1758 essay “The Way to Wealth”, where Father Abraham quotes it as “Poor Richard says.” Modern renderings tidy Franklin’s capitalisation and swap his semicolon for a comma, but the wording is authentically his.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labor wears, while the used key is always bright … But dost thou love life, then do not squander time, for that’s the stuff life is made of, as Poor Richard says.
trail: Quote databases and The Franklin Institute trace the line to Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1746, giving the wording “Dost thou love Life? then do not squander Time; for that’s the Stuff Life is made of.”
Wikiquote’s Poor Richard page lists the maxim among Franklin’s sourced almanac proverbs.
We read Franklin’s “The Way to Wealth” (1758) directly and confirmed the line appears verbatim, quoted as “Poor Richard says.”
source.excerptNote: From “The Way to Wealth” (1758), where Franklin has Father Abraham string together his best almanac maxims. The line first appeared, on its own, in the 1746 almanac.
source.rightsNote: Both Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1746 and “The Way to Wealth” (1758) were published in the eighteenth century — long before the 1931 U.S. copyright threshold — so the text is firmly in the public domain.

author.bio: Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) was a printer, scientist, diplomat and one of the founding fathers of the United States. From 1732 to 1758 he published Poor Richard’s Almanack under the pen name “Richard Saunders,” filling it with the pithy proverbs on thrift, industry and time that made him the most quoted American aphorist of the era. He gathered the best of them into his 1758 preface “The Way to Wealth,” which became one of the most widely reprinted texts of the eighteenth century.

misattribution.heading: A note on wording
misattribution.intro: Benjamin Franklin’s name is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for fabricated quotes, so healthy skepticism is warranted. In this case, though, the attribution is genuine — the only liberties modern quoters take are cosmetic.

items.why: The widely-shared form — “Dost thou love life? Then do not squander time, for that’s the stuff life is made of” — modernises Franklin’s capitalisation and replaces his semicolon with a comma. Franklin’s 1746 text reads “do not squander Time; for that’s the Stuff Life is made of,” per The Franklin Institute.
Unlike most feel-good lines pinned on Franklin, this one sits squarely in his documented work — both his 1746 almanac and his 1758 essay “The Way to Wealth.”

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: authentically Franklin. The thought and the wording are his, first printed in Poor Richard’s Almanack for 1746 and repeated in “The Way to Wealth” (1758).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Franklin ran Poor Richard’s Almanack for a quarter-century, seeding each edition with proverbs on thrift, diligence and the value of time. This line distils his signature theme: that time is not merely money but the very substance of a life.

In 1758 he harvested his favourite maxims into “The Way to Wealth,” a preface in which the fictional Father Abraham lectures a crowd entirely in Poor Richard’s sayings. Reprinted and translated for two centuries, it carried this line to a global audience and cemented Franklin’s reputation as America’s foremost aphorist.
context.pull: Time is not merely money — it is the stuff life is made of.
